extracted.intended_audience: students and readers studying Euclid's Elements / classical solid geometry
extracted.subtask_description: A sequence of propositions (theorems and constructions) from Euclid's Elements Book XI about the properties, construction, equality, and ratios of solid parallelepipeds, prisms, and solid angles. Each entry is a geometric statement followed by a synthetic proof or construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXIV — Opposite planes of six‑faced solid
rubrics_metrics.description: If a solid be contained by six planes, two and two of which are parallel; the opposite planes are similar and equal parallelograms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: show that common sections of parallel planes are parallel, deduce each face is a parallelogram, join appropriate diagonals and compare triangles formed; use equality of triangles and the fact parallelograms are doubles of corresponding triangles to conclude opposite parallelograms are equal and similar. (Full synthetic proof with diagram and stepwise equalities is provided.)

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXV — Ratio of solids from plane cut
rubrics_metrics.description: If a solid parallelepiped be cut by a plane parallel to two of its opposite planes, it divides the whole into two solids; the base of one of which shall be to the base of the other as the one solid is to the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction and proof: extend edges, form equimultiples of segments and corresponding parallelograms and solids; show equalities and equimultiples of bases correspond to equal multiples of the solids, hence base ratio equals solid ratio. Uses decomposition into equal solids via similar faces and equimultiples arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXVI (Problem) — Construct solid angle at a given point equal to a given solid angle
rubrics_metrics.description: At a given point in a given straight line, to make a solid angle equal to a given solid angle contained by three plane angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: from a point on given line erect perpendiculars and copy the three plane angles in the same order at the point, construct segments equal to corresponding edges (using right angles where needed), and join to form the required solid angle. Proof justifies equality by reducing to equalities of corresponding triangles and right angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXVII (Problem) — Describe parallelepiped similar and similarly situated
rubrics_metrics.description: To describe from a given straight line a solid parallelepiped similar and similarly situated to one given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: at an endpoint of the given line make a solid angle equal to that of the given parallelepiped, construct adjacent edges in proportions corresponding to the given solid's homologous sides, complete parallelograms and the solid; proof shows three faces correspond and opposite faces are equal so the constructed solid is similar and similarly situated to the given one.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXVIII — Plane through diagonals cuts parallelepiped equally
rubrics_metrics.description: If a solid parallelepiped be cut by a plane passing through the diagonals of two of the opposite planes, it shall be cut in two equal parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: show the two diagonals lie in a plane and are parallel; compare corresponding triangles and parallelograms on each side of the cutting plane and conclude the two solids formed are equal because they are contained by the same number of equal and similar planes, similarly situated and with solid angles not exceeding three plane angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXIX — Equal parallelepipeds on same base, same altitude (aligned terminations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Solid parallelepipeds upon the same base, and of the same altitude, the insisting straight lines of which are terminated in the same straight lines in the plane opposite to the base, are equal to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: consider cases where opposite parallelograms share a common side or not; cut solids by planes through diagonals to reduce to equal prisms or show equality by subtracting equal prisms. Uses decomposition and equality of contained prisms to prove the solids are equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXX — Equal parallelepipeds on same base, same altitude (general terminations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Solid parallelepipeds upon the same base, and of the same altitude, the insisting straight lines of which are not terminated in the same straight lines in the plane opposite to the base, are equal to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: extend insisting lines until they meet, form new parallelepiped(s) by joining intersection points, then show each original solid equals the constructed parallelepiped by previous proposition (XXIX), hence the two original solids equal one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXXI — Parallelepipeds on equal bases and same altitude are equal
rubrics_metrics.description: Solid parallelepipeds which are upon equal bases, and of the same altitude, are equal to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof covers several cases (insisting lines perpendicular to bases or not). Place bases in same plane, construct auxiliary parallelepipeds and use results of earlier propositions to show equality. When lines are not perpendicular, drop perpendiculars to reduce to parallelepipeds with right insisting lines and apply previous results; uses decompositions and equality arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXXII — Solids with same altitude are to one another as their bases
rubrics_metrics.description: Solid parallelepipeds which have the same altitude are to one another as their bases (i.e., solids are proportional to their bases when altitude equal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: construct an intermediate parallelepiped with base equal to one of the other bases and same altitude, show the ratios of solids reduce to ratios of bases by applying earlier proposition that cutting by planes parallel to opposite planes preserves ratios. Corollary: prisms on triangular bases of same altitude are to one another as their bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXXIII — Similar solids in triplicate ratio of homologous sides
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar solid parallelepipeds are to one another in the triplicate ratio of their homologous sides (i.e., ratio of volumes equals cube of ratio of homologous linear sides).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: produce homologous sides, take equal multiples to construct intermediate parallelepipeds; use chain of proportionalities among faces and solids to obtain four continuous proportionals, concluding the solid ratio is the triplicate ratio of the corresponding side ratio. Uses synthetic similar‑figures arguments and construction of continual proportionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. D — Ratio compounded of side ratios for equiangular solids
rubrics_metrics.description: Solid parallelepipeds contained by parallelograms equiangular to one another, each to each (i.e., solids whose solid angles are equal each to each), have to one another the ratio which is the same with the ratio compounded of the ratios of their sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: produce and take segments so faces become equal and similar to the other's faces, construct auxiliary solids and show by successive base/solid ratios that the ratio of the solids equals the compound ratio of the three corresponding side ratios (i.e., product of the three ratios). Uses the notion of compounded ratio and previous propositions about ratios of solids to bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXXIV — Bases and altitudes of equal solids reciprocally proportional
rubrics_metrics.description: The bases and altitudes of equal solid parallelepipeds are reciprocally proportional; and, conversely, if the bases and altitudes are reciprocally proportional, the solid parallelepipeds are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof handles cases where insisting lines are perpendicular to bases and where not. Shows that if solids equal then base1:base2 = altitude2:altitude1 (reciprocal), and conversely if bases and altitudes satisfy that reciprocal proportionality then solids are equal. Uses earlier propositions on solids proportional to their bases for equal altitude, construction of auxiliary solids, and perpendicular reductions.
